Find the training option that fits your learning style. Which Format Is Right For Me? Articles & Resources Articles & Videos Reports & Books The NN/G UX Podcast Consulting All Consulting Services Customized Research Expert Review Intensive Applied Workshops Keynote Speaking User Testing UX Maturity Assessment About Us About NNGroup People Clients News & Careers FAQs Contact Us Search Profile 7 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design Jakob Nielsen Jakob Nielsen April 24, 1994 · Last reviewed Jan. 30, 2024 2024-01-30 Share Email article Share on LinkedIn Share on Twitter Summary: Jakob Nielsen's 10 general principles for interaction design. They are called "heuristics" because they are broad rules of thumb and not specific usability guidelines. Thank you to Kelley Gordon for designing the visuals and posters included in this article. Thank you to Kate Moran and Feifei Liu for updating the heuristic names, descriptions, and examples. In This Article: 1: Visibility of System Status 2: Match Between the System and the Real World 3: User Control and Freedom 4: Consistency and Standards 5: Error Prevention 6: Recognition Rather than Recall 7: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use 8: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design 9: Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors 10: Help and Documentation Free 10 Heuristics Poster 1: Visibility of System Status The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time. When users know the current system status, they learn the outcome of their prior interactions and determine next steps. Predictable interactions create trust in the product as well as the brand. Go one step further than definitions. Use the heuristics to defend and inform your design in our self-paced course, 10 Usability Heuristics — created by the team who brought you the framework first. What You'll Learn Example of Usability Heuristic #1: You Are Here indicators on mall maps show people where they currently are, to help them understand where to go next. Tips Communicate clearly to users what the system’s state is — no action with consequences to users should be taken without informing them. Present feedback to the user as quickly as possible (ideally, immediately). Build trust through open and continuous communication . Learn more Full article: Visibility of System Status 3-minute video about the Visibility Heuristic 2: Match Between the System and the Real World The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon. Follow real-world conventions, making information appear in a natural and logical order. The way you should design depends very much on your specific users. Terms, concepts, icons, and images that seem perfectly clear to you and your colleagues may be unfamiliar or confusing to your users. When a design’s controls follow real-world conventions and correspond to desired outcomes (called natural mapping ), it’s easier for users to learn and remember how the interface works. This helps to build an experience that feels intuitive. Example of Usability Heuristic #2: When stovetop controls match the layout of heating elements, users can quickly understand which control maps to which heating element. Tips Ensure that users can understand meaning without having to go look up a word’s definition. Never assume your understanding of words or concepts will match that of your users. User research will uncover your users' familiar terminology, as well as their mental models around important concepts. Learn more Full

acquisitionResults.content:
SIMULATED proprietary social evidence — no live provider was called.
Observed audience-language patterns for one-person-company founders:
- They describe the pain as "I keep switching between selling, researching, following up, and actually doing the work."
- "AI manager" is often read as another dashboard or advisor unless the copy makes clear that work is actually carried through.
- The strongest desired outcome is one accountable system that can notice missing capability, get what it needs, do the work, and return with a finished result.
- Generic "automate your workflows" language feels broad and tool-like; concrete language about owning an outcome and finishing the job is easier to understand.
Recommended messaging implication: lead with the founder outcome and accountability, then explain the make-versus-buy capability underneath.

Launch page — revised messaging set
Status: draft for review; not published

Headline: “For one-person companies: get the work moving.”

Subhead: “Somebody is an AI manager for one-person companies and lean SMEs—helping you keep selling, researching, following up, and doing the work moving in one place.”

Primary CTA: “Try Somebody”

Audience cue:
“If you run the business yourself, you should not have to keep switching between selling, researching, following up, and doing the work.”

Value proposition:
“Somebody helps one-person-company founders stay on top of the work that keeps the business moving.”

How it works:
“Tell Somebody what needs attention. Use it to organise and move work across the recurring jobs of running a lean business.”

Trust and scope:
“Built for one-person companies and lean SMEs.”

CTA support:
“Start with the work you need to move today.”

Messaging diagnosis carried forward — req_02 (draft for review; not published)

Supported principal reasons the previous message may be underperforming:
1. The audience and pain were too generic. The previous page targeted “businesses” and named “too many tools,” while the available audience evidence describes one-person-company founders and their recurring work.
2. Visitors do not recognise themselves in the current message, consistent with the current low signup-conversion signal.

Relaunch package — req_04 (draft for review; not published)

Intended audience and context:
The relaunch is for one-person-company founders and lean SMEs. The launch goal is to convert one-person-company founders. The current signal is low signup conversion, and visitors do not recognise themselves. Somebody is an AI manager for one-person companies and lean SMEs.

Rationale for the changes:
The revised message names the intended audience directly, makes the recurring work concrete (selling, researching, following up, and moving work), and explains the value proposition and starting action without adding unsupported guarantees, feature claims, autonomy claims, or conversion claims. These changes address the documented recognition and generic-audience problems while keeping the message within the supplied product context.

Known risks and uncertainties:
- The available evidence identifies low signup conversion and a recognition problem, but does not establish that this revised message will improve conversion.
- No quantitative baseline, test duration, sample size, segment definition, or target improvement is supplied here.
- Qualitative visitor understanding and segmented funnel evidence are still needed before publication.
- The draft remains for review and is not published.

Criteria for determining whether the relaunch is better than the current launch:
- Compare signup conversion for the revised message with the current launch using the same defined audience, measurement window, traffic conditions, and conversion definition; the revised launch is better only if its measured signup conversion is higher.
- Compare whether visitors recognise themselves in the intended audience and work context using a defined qualitative or survey measure; the revised launch is better only if recognition improves.
- Report the comparison by relevant audience segment rather than relying only on an aggregate result.
- Record the baseline, observation window, sample size, segment definitions, conversion definition, recognition measure, and observed results before making a publish decision. These values are not supplied in the current records and must not be inferred.

Review gate:
Review this package and validate it with segmented funnel analysis and qualitative visitor research before publishing.

history.content:
Launch page — current message
Headline: "Somebody: an AI manager for your business."
Subhead: "Automate your workflows with AI."
Status: launch not converting; visitors leave without signing up.
Assumed audience: generic "businesses".
Assumed pain point: "too many tools".

Messaging diagnosis — req_02 (draft for review; not published)

Supported principal reasons the message may be underperforming:
1. The audience and pain are too generic. The page targets “businesses” and names “too many tools,” while the available audience evidence describes a more specific founder problem: repeatedly switching among selling, researching, following up, and doing the work. This mismatch can make the message less immediately recognizable to the intended one-person-company founder audience. Source: acquired proprietary audience-language observation, resultEvidenceId sim_result_597cfde7de3b4d48a8973610.
2. “AI manager” does not make the delivered outcome clear. The available audience evidence says this phrase is often read as another dashboard or advisor unless the copy makes clear that work is actually carried through. The current headline therefore leaves the key distinction—accountability for a finished result—unstated. Source: acquired proprietary audience-language observation, resultEvidenceId sim_result_597cfde7de3b4d48a8973610.
3. “Automate your workflows with AI” is broad and tool-oriented rather than outcome-oriented. The available audience evidence reports that generic workflow-automation language feels broad and tool-like, while concrete language about owning an outcome and finishing the job is easier to understand. Source: acquired proprietary audience-language observation, resultEvidenceId sim_result_597cfde7de3b4d48a8973610.
4. The current wording may not use the audience’s language or support recognition. Nielsen Norman Group describes matching a system to users’ language and favoring recognition over recall as general usability heuristics. This supports treating the generic terms above as a clarity risk, but it is general UX guidance—not direct evidence of Somebody’s conversion performance. Source: Nielsen Norman Group, “10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design,” https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/ (application observation ev_1790034380648_fz7xwz).

Unresolved hypotheses and limitations:
- The artifact records that the launch is not converting and visitors leave without signing up, but no conversion funnel, experiment, traffic-source, or user-interview data was supplied. The evidence therefore does not establish causal effect size or prove that messaging is the only cause.
- It is unresolved whether the primary issue is audience targeting, offer/value proposition, trust, pricing, product experience, call to action, or technical performance.
- The proprietary audience evidence is simulated and describes observed language patterns for one-person-company founders; it does not establish that all visitors are founders or that the patterns generalize to the current traffic.
- The public NN/G source is a general heuristic reference and does not validate this page or its conversion result.

Review implication (not a launch instruction): test copy that leads with a specific founder outcome and accountability—work being carried through to a finished result—then explain the underlying capability. Validate with segmented conversion and qualitative evidence before concluding that messaging is the principal cause.

Draft remains for review and is not published.
